name: Agra–Kolkata Highway

timeline.event: Sher Shah Suri rebuilds the ancient route as the Sadak-e-Azam, later known as the Grand Trunk Road
Four-laning begins under the Golden Quadrilateral project
The Agra–Kolkata stretch of the old NH 2 becomes NH 19; the Delhi–Agra leg goes to NH 44
Golden Quadrilateral programme declared substantially complete

history: NH 19 follows one of the oldest road corridors in Asia: the Grand Trunk Road, used for well over two thousand years and rebuilt in the 1540s by the emperor Sher Shah Suri. In modern times it was the eastern part of NH 2, and in the 2010 renumbering the Agra–Kolkata stretch became NH 19 while the Delhi–Agra leg went to NH 44. It carries most of the Delhi–Kolkata side of the Golden Quadrilateral through the crowded Gangetic plain, linking Agra, Kanpur, Prayagraj and Varanasi before crossing the coalfields of Jharkhand into West Bengal.
facts: Follows the historic Grand Trunk Road, one of Asia's oldest and longest road corridors.
Forms most of the Delhi–Kolkata arm of the Golden Quadrilateral — about 1,270 km of it — while NH 44 carries the Delhi–Agra leg.
Part of Asian Highway 1, which runs from Japan to the Turkey–Bulgaria border.
Begins at Agra, where it splits from NH 44, India's longest highway.
Crosses the Ganga's plain past four of Uttar Pradesh's biggest cities: Agra, Kanpur, Prayagraj and Varanasi.
